newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian govt says deregulation attracting miners.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian govt says deregulation attracting miners.

text.p: Deregulation of Tanzania's mining sector has spurred 40 multinational companies to take exploration licences for gold, diamonds and base metals and more than 100 applications are pending, government officials said.
Commissioner for Minerals Gray Mwakalukwa said reforms in the industry in 1992 had attracted between $30 million and $40 million of investment in exploration in Tanzanian sites.
More than 400 exploration licences had been granted by the ministry of water, energy and minerals since 1992 for exploration within an area of 800,000 square km.
He said mining to date was mostly artisanal or small-scale but the industry in Tanzania was in a state of transition.
"Apart from government (economic) incentives there's a conducive geological environment, political stability and lack of strife," Mwakalukwa told Reuters on Thursday.
Incentives on offer included tax exemption on equipment imports, guaranteed access to foreign exchange, repatriation of profits and security of tenure against nationalisation.
Another incentive was a 50-percent cut in standard corporate tax of 35 percent of the first four years of taxable income.

Mwakalukwa said royalties were also reduced and varied from 5.0 percent for diamonds to 3.0 percent for minerals including gold, silver and base metals and 1.0 percent for cut and polished diamonds or gemstones.
Australian, Canadian and South African companies lead the multinational pack, with exploration focused on gold and diamonds.
Tanzania's annual gold exports have fluctuated from 112 kg in 1989 to a peak of 4,525 kg in 1992. In 1994, 2,861 kg of gold was exported.
Privately, officials say the figures are conservative and that at least 50 percent more is smuggled out of the country.
Ministry figures put diamond exports at 75,885 carats in 1989, rising to a peak of 99,760 in 1991. Production in 1995 was 49,538 carats, of which about 80 percent were gem quality.
Most diamonds come from the Williamson mine at northern Mwadui in Shinyanga region.
While mining is a small contributor to Tanzania's GDP, it has risen gradually to 1.4 percent in 1995 from 0.3 percent in 1985.
